title: Effect: A Program Is a Value
subtitle: Build typed, lazy programs and run them at the edge
throughline: one number traveling as an Effect value: lifted into the success channel, wrapped and composed through the API, then run at the edge into a result.

chapters.title: A Program Is a Value
chapters.blurb: Meet the Effect type as a lazy, immutable blueprint with three channels, and see why it beats an eager Promise.

steps.title: A Program Is a Value
steps.coverSubtitle: Effect describes a program; it does not run it
steps.displayNarration: An `Effect` is a *lazy, immutable description* of a program. We follow one number through it, from blueprint to result.
steps.spoken: Before you run a single line, Effect asks you to describe your program as a value.

steps.title: The Promise problem
steps.displayNarration: A `Promise<A>` is *eager*: it starts the moment it is created, runs once, and its type only reveals the success value, never the errors.
steps.spoken: A Promise is eager. The instant you create it, the work starts, it runs exactly once, and its type tells you the value but hides every error it might throw.

steps.title: Effect is a blueprint
steps.displayNarration: An **Effect** is the opposite: a *lazily executed* blueprint. Creating it runs nothing; it merely models the work to be done.
steps.spoken: An Effect is the opposite. It is a blueprint that is executed lazily, so building it runs nothing at all. It simply models the work you want done.

steps.title: The success channel
steps.displayNarration: The blueprint carries three channels. The first, **A**, is the *Success* type — the value the program yields when it succeeds, like our `number`.
steps.spoken: That blueprint carries three channels. The first is A, the success type. It is the value the program hands back when everything goes right, like our number.

steps.title: The error channel
steps.displayNarration: The second channel, **E**, is the *Error* type — the expected failures, tracked statically instead of thrown and lost.
steps.spoken: The second channel is E, the error type. These are the expected failures, written right into the type instead of being thrown and lost at runtime.

steps.title: The requirements channel
steps.displayNarration: The third channel, **R**, is *Requirements* — the contextual dependencies the program needs, stored in a `Context` collection.
steps.spoken: The third channel is R, the requirements. These are the dependencies the program needs to run, gathered in a collection called the context.

steps.title: Effect of A, E, R
steps.displayNarration: Together they form `Effect<A, E, R>` — an immutable value where `never` means *cannot happen*: `Effect<number, never, never>` cannot fail and needs nothing.
steps.spoken: Together the three channels form Effect of A, E, R, one immutable value. The word never means cannot happen, so an Effect of number, never, never cannot fail and needs nothing.

steps.title: Pull the slots back out
steps.displayNarration: Given any effect, `Effect.Effect.Success`, `Effect.Effect.Error`, and `Effect.Effect.Context` *extract* each channel's type — the blueprint stays fully inspectable.
steps.spoken: And because it is just a value, you can read the slots back out. Success, Error, and Context utilities extract each channel's type, so the blueprint stays fully inspectable.

steps.title: Build now, run later
steps.displayNarration: The mental model: a `Promise` runs now; an **Effect** is a *typed blueprint* you build, inspect, and only later run at the edge.
steps.spoken: So here is the whole mental model. A Promise runs now and hides its errors. An Effect is a typed blueprint you build up, inspect, and only later choose to run at the edge.

chapters.title: Installing and Importing
chapters.blurb: Install one package, pick a named or namespace import, and learn why Effect ships standalone functions, not methods.

steps.title: Installing and Importing
steps.coverSubtitle: One package, two import styles, functions not methods
steps.displayNarration: Getting Effect into a project is one install. The whole core arrives in a single package.
steps.spoken: Getting Effect into your project takes a single command, and one package gives you the whole core.

steps.title: One package
steps.displayNarration: Run `npm install effect`. That one package gives you access to the *core functionality* of Effect — no à la carte modules to chase.
steps.spoken: Run npm install effect. That one package gives you the entire core of the library, so there are no extra modules to hunt down.

steps.title: The named import
steps.displayNarration: The common way is a **named import**: `import { Effect } from "effect"`. This is the heart of the library.
steps.spoken: The common way to reach it is a named import: import Effect from the effect package. That Effect module is the heart of the library.

steps.title: The namespace import
steps.displayNarration: You can also use a **namespace import**: `import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"`. Both forms expose the *same* API.
steps.spoken: You can also use a namespace import, pulling everything in as Effect from the effect slash Effect path. Both forms expose exactly the same API.

steps.title: The same module either way
steps.displayNarration: Both imports land on the same **Effect module**, which provides functions to *create, compose, and manipulate* effectful computations.
steps.spoken: Either way you land on the same Effect module, which provides the functions to create, compose, and manipulate your effectful computations.

steps.title: Functions, not methods
steps.displayNarration: Effect exposes *standalone functions*, not methods. Functions are **tree shakeable**, so a bundler can drop everything you never import.
steps.spoken: Crucially, Effect exposes standalone functions rather than methods. Functions are tree shakeable, so the bundler can drop every function you never import, leaving your build small.

steps.title: Why functions extend cleanly
steps.displayNarration: Functions also make the API *extensible*: you add your own helpers as plain functions, with no prototype patching. The namespace form especially aids weaker bundlers.
steps.spoken: Functions also keep the API extensible. You add your own helpers as plain functions, with no prototype patching, and the namespace form helps weaker bundlers shake the tree.

steps.title: A first effect
steps.displayNarration: Now build a first effect: `const program = Console.log("Hello, World!")`. It is still just a value — a blueprint waiting to run.
steps.spoken: Now you can build a first effect, a program that logs hello world. Remember, it is still just a value, a blueprint waiting to be run.

chapters.title: Creating Effects: Success and Failure
chapters.blurb: Lift known values and errors into the success and error channels with succeed, fail, and tagged errors.

steps.title: Creating Effects
steps.coverSubtitle: succeed lifts values, fail lifts errors
steps.displayNarration: Effect gives dedicated constructors for *both* outcomes: `Effect.succeed` and `Effect.fail`. Errors become values, not thrown exceptions.
steps.spoken: Effect gives you two dedicated constructors, one for success and one for failure, so errors become values you carry, not exceptions you throw.

steps.title: Start with a known value
steps.displayNarration: We begin with a plain value the program already has — the number `42` — ready to enter the effect world.
steps.spoken: We start with a value the program already holds, the number forty two, ready to step into the world of effects.

steps.title: Effect.succeed wraps it
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.succeed(42)` lifts that value into an effect that *always succeeds*. Its type is `Effect<number, never, never>`.
steps.spoken: Effect dot succeed lifts that value into an effect that always succeeds. Its type is Effect of number, never, never, meaning it cannot fail and needs nothing.

steps.title: Effect.fail puts a value in E
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.fail(error)` does the mirror image: it places a *recoverable* error into the **E** channel, giving `Effect<never, E>`.
steps.spoken: Effect dot fail does the mirror image. It places a recoverable error into the E channel, producing an effect of never, E, an effect that only ever fails.

steps.title: Errors are values
steps.displayNarration: Because the failure rides the E channel instead of being *thrown*, it keeps propagating until you handle it — nothing is silently lost.
steps.spoken: Because that failure rides the error channel instead of being thrown, it keeps propagating until you choose to handle it. Nothing slips away unnoticed.

steps.title: Tagged errors
steps.displayNarration: A tidy error is a **tagged error**: `class HttpError extends Data.TaggedError("HttpError")<{}> {}` carries a `_tag` you can match on later.
steps.spoken: For tidy errors, you reach for a tagged error. Data dot tagged error builds a class that carries a tag field, a label you can match on later when handling failures.

steps.title: Both outcomes in the type
steps.displayNarration: Combine them and the signature tells the whole story: `Effect<number, Error>` — succeeds with a `number` *or* fails with an `Error`, statically.
steps.spoken: Put the two together and the signature tells the whole story. Effect of number, Error means the program either succeeds with a number or fails with an error, and the compiler knows both.

steps.title: Explicit success and failure
steps.displayNarration: Both paths are explicit and type-tracked: `succeed` lifts a value into **A**, `fail` lifts an error into **E**, and the caller sees every outcome.
steps.spoken: So success and failure are both explicit and tracked in the type. Succeed lifts a value into A, fail lifts an error into E, and anyone calling your code sees every possible outcome.

chapters.title: Wrapping Side Effects
chapters.blurb: Bring existing sync and Promise code into Effect with sync, try, promise, and tryPromise.

steps.title: Wrapping Side Effects
steps.coverSubtitle: Bring sync and Promise code into the typed world
steps.displayNarration: Real code already has side effects. Effect provides constructors that take a *thunk* and bring that code into the typed effect world.
steps.spoken: Your real code already has side effects. Effect gives you constructors that take a deferred function, a thunk, and bring that existing code into the typed world.

steps.title: Start from a thunk
steps.displayNarration: Each constructor accepts a **thunk** — a zero-argument function like `() => A` — so the computation is *deferred* until the effect runs.
steps.spoken: Each of these constructors accepts a thunk, a function that takes no arguments. Wrapping the work in a thunk defers it, so nothing happens until the effect actually runs.

steps.title: Effect.sync for safe work
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.sync(() => {...})` defers synchronous work you *know* won't throw, like `console.log`. It yields `Effect<A, never, never>`.
steps.spoken: Effect dot sync defers synchronous work you are sure will not throw, like writing to the console. The result is an effect that cannot fail.

steps.title: A throw becomes a defect
steps.displayNarration: If a `sync` thunk *does* throw, that is treated as a **defect** — an unrecoverable flaw, like an unexpected crash, not an expected error.
steps.spoken: But if that sync thunk does throw, Effect treats it as a defect. A defect is an unrecoverable flaw, like an unexpected crash, not the kind of error you planned for.

steps.title: Effect.try captures a throw
steps.displayNarration: When a thunk *might* throw, use `Effect.try(() => JSON.parse(input))`. It catches the throw and surfaces it as an `UnknownException` in the E channel.
steps.spoken: When a thunk might throw, reach for Effect dot try. It captures the thrown error and surfaces it as an unknown exception in the error channel, so the failure is no longer lost.

steps.title: Remap into a typed error
steps.displayNarration: The `{ try, catch }` overload lets you *remap* the caught value into your own error, turning `UnknownException` into a precise `Effect<A, E>`.
steps.spoken: And with the try and catch overload, you remap the caught value into your own error type, turning that generic unknown exception into a precise, typed error of your choosing.

steps.title: Effect.promise for safe async
steps.displayNarration: For asynchronous work, `Effect.promise(() => Promise<A>)` wraps a Promise you *trust* to resolve. A reject here also becomes a *defect*.
steps.spoken: For asynchronous work, Effect dot promise wraps a Promise you trust to always resolve. Just like sync, if it unexpectedly rejects, that becomes a defect.

steps.title: Effect.tryPromise for risky async
steps.displayNarration: When a Promise *may* reject, use `Effect.tryPromise(() => fetch(...))`. Rejections are caught into `UnknownException`, or remapped via `{ try, catch }`.
steps.spoken: When a Promise may reject, like a network fetch, use Effect dot tryPromise. Rejections are caught into an unknown exception, or remapped to a typed error, so failures finally surface in E instead of being lost.

chapters.title: Composing and Running
chapters.blurb: Build pipelines with pipe and gen, combine effects, then run them at the edge with runPromise, runSync, or runFork.

steps.title: Composing and Running
steps.coverSubtitle: Build the pipeline, then run it at the edge
steps.displayNarration: Now we *compose* small effects into one program with `pipe` or `Effect.gen`, then run it. Until a `run*` call, everything stays inert.
steps.spoken: Now we compose our small effects into one program, using either pipelines or generators, and finally run it. Until that run call, everything stays inert.

steps.title: pipe reads left to right
steps.displayNarration: `pipe` replaces nested `f(g(h(x)))` with a readable left-to-right sequence, feeding each result into the next step.
steps.spoken: The pipe function replaces nested calls, where you read inside out, with a clean left to right sequence. The output of one step becomes the input of the next.

steps.title: map transforms the value
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.map` applies a function to the value inside the effect, returning a *new* effect with the transformed `A` — effects are immutable.
steps.spoken: Inside the pipeline, Effect dot map applies a function to the value inside the effect. Because effects are immutable, it returns a brand new effect with the transformed value.

steps.title: flatMap chains effects
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.flatMap` chains a function that *returns another effect*, flattening the result so you avoid nested `Effect<Effect<...>>`.
steps.spoken: Effect dot flatMap is for chaining. When your next step itself returns an effect, flatMap runs it and flattens the result, so you never end up with effects nested inside effects.

steps.title: tap for side effects
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.tap` runs a side effect — like `Console.log` — then *passes the original value through* unchanged. `Effect.all` would instead combine many effects, short-circuiting on the first failure.
steps.spoken: Effect dot tap runs a side effect, like logging, then passes the original value straight through unchanged. A sibling, Effect dot all, combines many effects at once and stops on the first failure.

steps.title: Effect.gen, the async/await style
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.gen(function* () { ... })` gives async/await-style code: each `yield*` *binds* an effect's result and short-circuits the whole block on failure.
steps.spoken: If you prefer, Effect dot gen gives you async await style code. Inside the generator, each yield star binds the result of an effect, and if any of them fails, the whole block short circuits.

steps.title: One composed, inert program
steps.displayNarration: Either path produces a single **composed effect** — and it is *still inert*. No work has happened yet; it is only a richer blueprint.
steps.spoken: Both paths fold everything down into one composed effect. And it is still completely inert. No work has run yet. It is just a richer blueprint than before.

steps.title: Run it at the edge
steps.displayNarration: Finally, run at the *edge*: `Effect.runPromise` (preferred) returns a `Promise`, `Effect.runSync` runs pure sync work, and `Effect.runFork` starts it in the background as a fiber.
steps.spoken: Finally you run it at the edge of your program. Run promise is the preferred choice and gives you a promise. Run sync handles pure synchronous work. And run fork starts it in the background as a fiber.

steps.title: Build now, run once
steps.displayNarration: The whole journey: lift a value, compose it through `pipe` or `gen`, and trigger it *once* with a `run*` call that turns the blueprint into a real result.
steps.spoken: And that is the whole journey. You lift a value, compose it through pipelines or generators into one program, and trigger it just once with a run call that finally turns the blueprint into a real result.

chapters.title: Requirements: filling the R channel
chapters.blurb: Why runPromise can't run an Effect until the R channel is empty — and how provide and a Layer fill it.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.coverSubtitle: Nothing runs until the R channel is empty
steps.displayNarration: The third slot of `Effect<A, E, R>` is **R** — the services a program still needs. `Effect.runPromise` won't run it until R is `never`.
steps.spoken: The third slot of an Effect is R, the requirements: the services a program still needs. And run promise will not run that program until the R channel is empty.

steps.title: A program that needs a service
steps.displayNarration: When a program does `yield* Random` inside `Effect.gen`, its type becomes `Effect<number, never, Random>` — the **R** slot now lists `Random`, a service it can't supply itself.
steps.spoken: When a program reaches for a service, say a Random service, that service shows up in its type. The third slot, R, now lists Random: a dependency the program cannot supply on its own.

steps.title: R is a ledger of what's missing
steps.displayNarration: Every `Context.Tag` you `yield*` is added to **R** and stays there until something provides it. R is the running list of unmet requirements.
steps.spoken: Every service the program reaches for is added to R, and stays there until something provides it. R is just a running list of the requirements that haven't been met yet.

steps.title: runPromise refuses to run
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.runPromise` only accepts `Effect<A, E, never>`. While `Random` is still in **R**, running the program is a *type error* — it can't even start.
steps.spoken: Now try to run it. Run promise only accepts an Effect whose R is never, meaning no outstanding requirements. While Random is still in R, this is a type error, and the program simply will not start.

steps.title: Build the service with a Layer
steps.displayNarration: To satisfy **R**, describe how to build the service: `Layer.succeed(Random, { next: Effect.succeed(0.5) })` is a blueprint for a live `Random`.
steps.spoken: To satisfy R, you describe how to build the service. A Layer is that blueprint. Layer dot succeed wires up a real Random implementation, ready to be handed to the program.

steps.title: provide discharges the requirement
steps.displayNarration: `Effect.provide(program, RandomLive)` injects the service and removes `Random` from **R** — the channel collapses back to `never`.
steps.spoken: Effect dot provide injects that service into the program and removes Random from R. With nothing left to require, the R channel collapses back to never.

steps.title: R = never, so it runs
steps.displayNarration: Now `Effect.runPromise(runnable)` is allowed — the requirements are met, so it executes and returns a `Promise<number>`.
steps.spoken: Now run promise is allowed, because the requirements are met and R is never. The program finally executes, and returns a promise of a number.

steps.title: Inert until every requirement is met
steps.displayNarration: The rule: `runPromise` (and `runSync`) demand `R = never`. Track needs in **R**, satisfy them with `provide` or a `Layer`, and only then does the program run.
steps.spoken: So the rule is simple. Run promise, and run sync, demand that R is never. Your program tracks what it needs in R, you satisfy those needs with provide or a layer, and only then does it actually run.
